title: Part One, Chapter 8: The Death of Sipacua

verses.t: Here follows how Sipacua was defeated and killed, and how he too was defeated by the two boys, Hun-ahpu and Xbalanque. What wounded their hearts was the killing of the four hundred boys who were killed by Sipacua. And this one looked only for fish and crabs along the banks of the rivers, and this was what he ate every day; by day he wandered about looking for his food, and by night he carried mountains on his back. Then Hun-ahpu and Xbalanque made an image of a crab out of a leaf that grows on the trees, called ec; they made the crab's big claws from it, and the small ones from other, smaller leaves called pahac, and they made the shell and claws out of flat stone. And they set it up; they put it in a cave beneath a great mountain called Meaban, where he was defeated. And then the boys came and met Sipacua, as if by chance, at the stream, and they asked him, "Where are you going, boy?" And Sipacua said, "I am not going anywhere; I am only looking for my food." And they asked him, "What is your food?" "Only fish and crabs, and I have not found any, and I have not eaten since the day before yesterday, and I can no longer bear the hunger." And then they said to him, "There is a crab down there at the bottom of the ravine, and truly it is very big. How good it would be if you ate it! We tried to catch it, and it bit us, and we were afraid of it. Or, if you like, shall we go and catch it?" "Have pity on me; take me to where it is," said Sipacua. "We do not want to," they said, "but go on; you will not get lost. Go upstream and you will come straight to it. It is making a noise beneath a great mountain, going 'hovol,' and you will go straight there," said Hun-ahpu and Xbalanque. "Oh, poor me! Did you not find it, then?" said Sipacua. "I shall go and show you where there are many birds for you to shoot with the blowgun; only I know where they are." And before their eyes the crab went in under the stone slab. "And can you really catch it? Do not make us go back for nothing, for we tried to catch it and could not; when we lay down and went in, it bit us, and we very nearly caught it. So it will be good for you to go in after it from below." "Very well," said Sipacua. And then they went with him, and they came beneath the ravine, and the crab was lying on its side with its shell bright red; and there beneath the ravine was the boys' trick. "Very well," said Sipacua, rejoicing, and he longed to eat it, for he was starving; and he tried to go in lying down, and the crab kept moving upwards, and it came out again. And the boys said to him, "Didn't you catch it?" "I didn't catch it; I almost caught it, but it went up higher, so perhaps it will be best to go in from above." And then he went in from above, and he got all the way in, until only his knees were left to go in, when the mountain crumbled and settled gently down upon his chest, and he never came back; and Sipacua turned into stone. And so Sipacua was defeated by the boys Hun-ahpu and Xbalanque; and they say that this eldest son of Vucub-caquix was the one who made the mountains in ancient times. Beneath the mountain called Meaban he was defeated, and only by a miracle was he defeated. And now we shall tell of the other one who grew proud.
